tier_reason: First-party study with public harness and raw JSON (bench/runtime-corpus-study.md, bench/results/runtime-corpus-{amd64,arm64}.json, bench/startup/run.mjs) naming both CPUs and every engine version, but neither the study nor the startup sweep states the Go toolchain or the build command and flags used for the wago CLI and the Go adapters, so it falls short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'compile 5x quicker and execute 1.9x faster than wazero' (these figures point at wago.sh, which is blocked, and are not reproduced by any committed data). Committed bench/runtime-corpus-study.md geometric means on Ryzen 7 7800X3D: compile wall wago 6.42 ms vs wazero 7.83, wasmtime 9.77, V8 14.44, wasmer 14.80 ms; cold execute wago 7.34 ms vs wazero 8.11, wasmtime 7.56, V8 16.84, wasmer 10.88, wasm3 9.91, wasmi 12.34 ms. On Apple M4 Max: compile wago 4.43 ms vs wazero 5.32, wasmtime 7.12, V8 14.75, wasmer 8.91; cold execute wago 4.77 ms vs wazero 5.27, wasmtime 5.95, V8 15.59, wasmer 6.76. So about 1.2x to 3.3x faster compile and 1.03x (wasmtime, AMD64) to 3.3x (V8, ARM64) lower cold execute latency (derived from page data). From the committed JSON, wago's internal Go-side compile time is a geometric mean 0.32x of wazero's on AMD64 and 0.43x on ARM64 over 63 modules (derived from page data). The separate committed startup sweep (bench/startup/startup-{amd64,arm64}.json, hyperfine -N, 6 Rust compute twins run from _start) gives wago end-to-end geometric means of 0.77x wazero, 0.62x wasmtime and 0.30x V8 on AMD64 and 0.75x wazero, 0.74x wasmtime and 0.30x V8 on ARM64 (derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Engine versions listed (wasmtime 45.0.1/46.0.1, wasmer 7.1.0/7.3.0, V8 15.1.42/15.2.20, wazero 1.12.0 adapter, wasm3 0.9.0/0.5.0, wasmi_cli 1.1.0, WAVM prerelease, wazy 0.3.0). bench/go.mod at the study commit 7c382581 pins toolchain go1.22.2, but the study does not say how the wago CLI and the Go adapters were built; build flags not stated.
corrections.caveats: Cold-start wall times include process start, so the large wins over V8 and WAVM partly reflect the CLI startup cost of those engines, and wago/wazero/wazy run through single-purpose Go adapters while the others use their native CLIs; the execute metric includes compile and only the first export call. Wago's cold execute is within noise of Wasmtime on AMD64 (7.34 vs 7.56 ms geomean) and loses to it on several PolyBench modules (floyd-warshall 14.00 vs 9.90 ms, seidel-2d 11.39 vs 10.28 ms); the wasm3 and wasmi interpreters beat wago on many small AMD64 cold-execute cases (tiny 4.28/4.15 vs 6.33 ms). Wazy, another pure-Go compiler, is within about 5-15% of wago. Compute-heavy steady-state speed was not isolated in the corpus study. The README's 5x and 1.9x figures point at wago.sh (blocked) and do not match any committed data. Three AssemblyScript modules are execution gaps for every engine. First-party benchmark (harness, JSON and study are public, CPUs named, Go build not documented), so held at C. Version is 0.0.0 beta.

notes: Every number in claimed_speedup checks out against the study and the raw JSON; I recomputed the 0.32x internal-compile geomean (0.324 AMD64, 0.426 ARM64) and added the separate bench/startup hyperfine sweep. Shortcomings: the README's 5x/1.9x headline is unbacked by committed data; cold-start numbers are dominated by process startup; wasmtime matches or beats it on AMD64 cold execute; Go build not documented. wago.sh is EGRESS_BLOCKED.

tier_reason: The README Metrics section gives first-party op/s numbers against wabt and Binaryen, produced by public code (test/bench.js), but names no CPU, browser or Node version, so it is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README metrics: watr 3,123 op/s versus wabt 859 op/s (about 3.6x, derived from page data), Binaryen 473 op/s (about 6.6x), the WebAssembly spec wast.js 1,509 op/s and wat-compiler 355 op/s. Optimizer table (wasm-opt 128, 21 modules in test/example): watr/optimize about 110 ms in-process for the batch versus wasm-opt -Oz 990 ms as a CLI run (about 9x, but includes process spawn), with total output 19,734 B against 19,852 B for -Oz and 22,302 B for -O3.
corrections.caveats: Benchmark code is public (test/bench.js, browser-run, single brownian.wat input, N=500, no warmup, no check that outputs match) but the README gives no CPU, browser or Node version. wabt and Binaryen are measured as their JavaScript/Wasm builds, not as native CLIs. The wabt path (test/util.js wat2wasm) calls toBinary with log: true, which makes wabt build a binary-writer log on every iteration; that probably inflates wabt's time, though by how much was not measured. For a 5.5 MB module the README itself says Binaryen's native core is faster (0.44 s versus about 2.6 s optimize plus 0.19 s compile). The 110 ms versus 990 ms optimizer comparison pits an in-process call against a spawned CLI. The LICENSE is MIT and is also offered under the Krishnized License.

notes: README numbers and bench code match the record. New shortcoming: the wabt baseline runs with toBinary({log: true}) in test/util.js, a likely handicap to the baseline. Other flaws: no hardware or runtime stated, one input file, no warmup. Metadata is correct: 74 stars, MIT, last commit 2026-10-01.

tier_reason: StarlingMonkey PR #91 (merged 2024-07-31) reports Richards 676 with weval versus 189 without, using a stated build command but no hardware or Wasmtime version. The peer-reviewed PLDI 2025 paper is visible only as search snippets, since cfallin.org, arXiv and the ACM DL are blocked, so it is held at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: '3-5x speedups over the generic interpreter' (no methodology). StarlingMonkey PR #91 (merged 2024-07-31) quotes Richards score 676 with weval AOT versus 189 for the plain interpreter (about 3.6x, derived from page data). The PLDI 2025 paper 'Partial Evaluation, Whole-Program Compilation' (Fallin and Bernstein, PACMPL 9 PLDI, article 160) reports 2.17x on SpiderMonkey and 1.84x on PUC-Rio Lua over the generic interpreters (search snippet only).
corrections.caveats: The baseline is the project's own interpreter without weval, not a rival runtime, so the speedup says nothing about how Wasmtime or V8 compare. The README gives a range without methodology, and the PR states neither hardware nor the Wasmtime version. The peer-reviewed paper (cfallin.org PDF, arXiv 2411.10559, ACM DL 10.1145/3729259) was blocked from this environment, so the 2.17x/1.84x averages come from search snippets only and the tier is held at C; once the paper can be read it is a candidate for B. The licence is Apache-2.0 with the LLVM exception.

notes: Confirmed the PR numbers and the README claim. Licence corrected to Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception (Cargo.toml and LICENSE). The PLDI 2025 paper is real (two search snippets agree on 2.17x SpiderMonkey and 1.84x Lua), but its PDF is EGRESS_BLOCKED, so it is a paper-access retier candidate for B. Shortcoming: the baseline is its own unspecialized interpreter, with no hardware stated.
